summary: Karan Sampath, a forward-deployed engineer at Anthropic, presents the case for gateways as the solution to enterprise MCP challenges. He identifies three critical hurdles: observability (tracking tool usage, performance, and how tools are defined), access control (scoping server and tool access to correct users, teams, and agents), and security (verifying server safety, preventing data exfiltration, managing untrusted clients). He calls these a "three-headed hydra." Despite a growing registry of thousands of servers, enterprises struggle to deploy more than a handful due to these gaps. Security teams become overloaded, and the bottleneck restricts agent effectiveness. The core intuition is that security teams must bless one platform to establish a root of trust enabling decentralized MCP development. Gateways serve as this middleware layer between MCP servers and clients, handling auth, authorization, observability, secure connectivity, and deployment. Components include auth, role-based access control, proxy routing, secure tunnels, a sub-registry, and a CLI. Once a gateway is in place, enterprises gain follow-on benefits: easy multi-surface integration (claude.ai, Claude core), encrypted secured connections, faster team iteration without repeated security reviews, standard primitives encoding enterprise operating procedures, pluggable credentials supporting company-wide, team-wide, or service accounts, and scalability from tens to hundreds of thousands of agents. Looking forward, Anthropic envisions decoupling the agent harness from where data lives, so agents are not tightly coupled to data or MCP structure. This gives enterprises flexibility to choose which agents to keep in-house versus external while the gateway remains invariant. Sampath concludes with three takeaways: invest in common infrastructure rather than rolling your own MCPs, use gateways for secured connections to build root of trust, and work toward separating agent architecture from the data layer.

sections.title: Introduction and Speaker Background
sections.summary: Karan Sampath introduces himself as a forward-deployed engineer at Anthropic, the first outside the US, working with enterprises on MCPs and internal use cases. He outlines the talk's focus on enterprise MCP problems, gateways as the solution, and alignment with Anthropic's future vision for agent tech deployments.

sections.title: Enterprise Hurdles: The Three-Headed Hydra
sections.summary: Sampath identifies three major enterprise hurdles with MCPs: observability (tracking who uses tools and how), access control (scoping server and tool access to correct user groups), and security (verifying server safety, preventing data exfiltration, managing untrusted clients). He calls these a "three-headed hydra" and notes they are table stakes the community hasn't adequately addressed.

sections.title: Registry Gaps and Deployment Bottlenecks
sections.summary: Despite a growing registry of thousands of servers, registries are incomplete for enterprises—lacking authentication, access control, observability, and credential management. Teams can build MCPs but cannot deploy them due to security team overload and access issues. This bottleneck restricts the protocol and hurts agent effectiveness, keeping enterprises at single-digit MCP usage.

sections.title: The Case for Gateways: Establishing a Root of Trust
sections.summary: The core intuition is that security teams must bless one platform to establish a root of trust, enabling decentralized MCP development. Enterprises that do this can explore MCP usage and unlock agent power. Since every good MCP helps all agents, this investment has exponential knock-on effects.

sections.title: Gateway Definition and Core Components
sections.summary: A gateway is defined as a middleware layer between numerous MCP servers and any MCP client, handling auth, authorization, observability, secure connectivity, and deployment. Components include auth, role-based access control, proxy routing, secure tunnels, a sub-registry, and a CLI. This lets teams focus only on business logic when building new MCP servers.

sections.title: Strategic Benefits: Authentication and Delegated Identity
sections.summary: Gateways provide easy authentication by plugging into existing IDPs and enable delegated identity for both users and agents. Access control can be scoped by team, user, or employee. Observability extends beyond usage metrics to understanding how tools are defined and adapting load-bearing tools to agent needs. Anthropic sees novel definitions of agent identity as increasingly important.

sections.title: Operational Gains: Multi-Surface, Security, and Scalability
sections.summary: Sampath outlines six follow-on benefits of gateways: (1) easy multi-surface integration—MCP servers plug into claude.ai, Claude core, and Claude core work via one gateway; (2) encrypted secured connections preventing data exfiltration; (3) faster iteration—teams develop workflows without repeated security reviews; (4) standard primitives encoding enterprise operating procedures; (5) pluggable credentials supporting company-wide, team-wide, or service accounts; (6) scalability from tens to hundreds of thousands of agents. He notes open-source examples exist and offers to help enterprises implement this.

sections.title: Future Vision: Decoupling Agent Architecture from Data Layers
sections.summary: Anthropic's larger vision is separating the agent harness from where data lives. With an explosion of agents, agents shouldn't be tightly coupled to data structure or MCP structure. As an example, an MCP gateway can connect to Claude managed agents or be used internally with the Claude agent SDK. This gives enterprises flexibility to decide which agents to keep in-house versus external while the gateway remains invariant, allowing strong investment in opinionated gateway primitives.

sections.title: Summary: Invest in Common Infrastructure
sections.summary: Sampath concludes with three takeaways: invest in common infrastructure rather than rolling your own MCPs; use gateways for secured connections to build root of trust; and work toward separating the agent harness from the data layer. He invites further conversation with interested parties.
